hints: Compare the structures carefully and notice what is lost from citric acid and what appears in the final product.
Stage 1 removes the tertiary -OH group along with a neighbouring H, so Q must contain a C=C double bond formed by dehydration.
Once you have an alkene intermediate, think which reagent adds hydrogen across C=C while leaving the three -COOH groups untouched.
walkthrough:
**Spot the overall change**

Look side by side at the two acids. Citric acid has a central $\text{C-OH}$ group, while tricarballylic acid has a central $\text{C-H}$ group in the same place.

All three $\text{-COOH}$ groups are unchanged, so overall we are replacing $\text{-OH}$ by $\text{-H}$.

**Work out stage 1 to make Q**

A tertiary alcohol like this is easily dehydrated by heating with concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to form an alkene plus water.

$$\text{R}_2\text{C(OH)-CH}_2\text{R} \rightarrow \text{R}_2\text{C=CHR} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

So Q is the unsaturated tricarboxylic acid, often called aconitic acid.

**Work out stage 2 to finish**

Q now contains a $\text{C=C}$ bond that must be converted to $\text{CH-CH}_2$. This is catalytic hydrogenation.

$$\text{>C=C<} + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} \text{>CH-CH<}$$

$\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ with Ni catalyst does this cleanly and does not reduce carboxylic acids.

options.A: Concentrated H2SO4 in stage 1 dehydrates the tertiary alcohol to the alkene Q, and H2 with Ni in stage 2 hydrogenates the C=C to give tricarballylic acid. Both reagents are selective and leave COOH groups intact.
options.B: Stage 1 is correct, but LiAlH4 in stage 2 is wrong. LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent that reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols, so it would destroy the three COOH groups instead of just hydrogenating C=C.
options.C: LiAlH4 in stage 1 is wrong because it would reduce the COOH groups rather than dehydrate the alcohol. Aqueous H2SO4 in stage 2 would hydrate an alkene, not reduce it to an alkane.
options.D: NaOH(aq) in stage 1 would simply neutralise the carboxylic acids to form carboxylate salts, not dehydrate the alcohol to an alkene. Stage 2 alone cannot then give the required product.
